ddx.step1_summary:
- Chief complaint: Severe headache for ~3 days.
- Symptoms: Onset ~3 days ago, gradual onset at work; located all over head but mainly around right eye; constant with fluctuating severity (worse at times); pain described as dull with intermittent sharper episodes; severity 8/10. Associated photophobia (light hurts), transient "shooting lights" at onset, feeling sick/nausea but no vomiting, difficulty focusing. No neck stiffness, no focal neurological deficits, no recent head injury. Headache worse with screen/bright light. Ibuprofen taken (about 3 tablets/day for last 2 days) with minimal benefit; reduced screen brightness helps somewhat. Patient wonders about dehydration/stress as triggers.
- Past medical history: Reported otherwise fit and well; no chronic illnesses mentioned.
- Medications / Allergies: No regular medications. Took oral ibuprofen recently. No known drug allergies.
- Family / Social history: Mother and sister have frequent migraines (family history positive). Lives with housemates. Works in IT (lots of computer/screen time). Wears glasses since childhood. Social smoker and drinks alcohol socially. Contraceptive status unclear from transcript.
- Vital signs / Exam findings: No vitals recorded in transcript. No focal neurological deficits reported on history. No fever reported. No rash. No neck stiffness on exam (patient denied).
- Labs / Imaging: None mentioned or performed.

V: Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH): Presents with severe headache and photophobia/visual symptoms. Rationale: severe headache (8/10) and worsening over days could raise vascular concerns, though classic SAH is sudden thunderclap and usually has neck stiffness/ vomiting which are absent here.

Carotid/vertebral artery dissection: Can cause unilateral periorbital/head pain and visual symptoms. Rationale: unilateral right-sided/periorbital pain could fit, though there is no history of trauma or focal neuro signs.
I: Meningitis/encephalitis: Can present with headache, photophobia, nausea, and neck stiffness. Rationale: headache + photophobia could fit but absence of fever, neck stiffness, and systemic illness makes this unlikely.

Acute sinusitis: Frontal/periorbital pain and headache that can be worse around the eyes. Rationale: periorbital pain location could reflect sinus involvement, but no nasal symptoms or fever recorded.
N: Intracranial mass/space-occupying lesion: Progressive headache, worse on waking and cognitive difficulty can be features. Rationale: worsening over days and difficulty focusing raise a remote possibility, though presentation is more acute and lacks focal deficits or other red flags.
D: Tension-type headache: Bilateral/diffuse dull pressure-type pain related to stress and prolonged screen use. Rationale: works in IT with prolonged computer exposure and recent work stress; pain described as dull and worsening with focus/screen brightness.
Dehydration / simple metabolic cause: Can cause diffuse headache. Rationale: patient suspects poor hydration as a trigger.
I2: Medication-overuse headache: Chronic analgesic use can worsen headaches. Rationale: patient has taken ibuprofen recently, but duration and frequency are insufficient for typical medication-overuse headache (usually >2–3 months of frequent use).
Caffeine withdrawal/intoxication: Can cause headache and nausea. Rationale: social habits not detailed; possible but not supported by transcript.
C: None likely relevant: No congenital conditions suggested by history. (No plausible congenital cause identified from transcript.)
A: Allergic rhinitis causing sinus headache: Allergies can lead to sinus congestion and periorbital pain. Rationale: periorbital pain could be sinus-related, but patient denied rashes or allergy symptoms.
T: Recent head trauma-related headache / post-concussive: Traumatic causes can produce headaches. Rationale: patient denies recent head injury, so traumatic causes are unlikely.
E: Hormonal migraine (menstrual or hormone-related): Hormonal fluctuations can trigger migraines in young women. Rationale: patient is female of reproductive age; family history of migraine; contraceptive status not clearly stated.
Metabolic (hypoglycemia) or hypertensive headache: Could cause headache but lacks specific supporting evidence (no BP or glucose documented).

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: History strongly consistent with migraine: severe unilateral-predominant periorbital headache (right eye), photophobia (light sensitivity), transient visual phenomena described as "shooting lights" (possible aura), nausea/feeling sick, family history of migraine (mother and sister), aggravation by light and screen, poor response to OTC ibuprofen. Age and female sex also fit common migraine demographics.
supporting_evidence: Photophobia — "light is quite annoying, my eyes... it hurts"
Visual phenomena — "weird shooting lights" at onset
Family history of migraines (mother and sister)
Severe pain (8/10) and poor response to ibuprofen
opposing_evidence: No prior personal history of classic migraine (patient reports never had migraines before)
No clear pulsatile/throbbing description (patient described mainly dull)
No aura clearly delineated timing-wise (patient described lights but not a typical evolving aura)
No formal neurologic exam or red flag symptoms documented, but absence does not exclude migraine

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Tension-type headache / cervicogenic or stress-related headache
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Dull, diffuse head pain and relationship to work stress and prolonged computer use support tension-type headache or eye strain. Patient works in IT, reports difficulty focusing and relieved somewhat by reducing screen brightness. Prior headaches that responded to ibuprofen could have been tension-type. However photophobia, visual phenomena, and nausea are less typical of pure tension headache.
supporting_evidence: Dull quality of pain and diffuse location
Work-related stress (starting a new project) and prolonged screen exposure
Longstanding need for glasses and reduced screen brightness improves symptoms
Previous headaches that responded to ibuprofen
opposing_evidence: Prominent photophobia and visual "shooting lights" are more typical of migraine
Associated nausea and severity (8/10) are less typical for uncomplicated tension-type headache

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Eyestrain / computer vision syndrome (refractive error-related headache)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Working long hours on screens with glasses since childhood and difficulty focusing suggests possible uncorrected or outdated refractive error causing chronic eye strain headache. Reducing screen brightness provided some relief. However the presence of photophobia, visual phenomena and significant nausea point more toward migraine than pure eyestrain.
supporting_evidence: IT work with prolonged screen use and difficulty focusing
Wears glasses since age 5 and reports no recent eye test
opposing_evidence: Shooting lights and photophobia are not typical of simple refractive eyestrain
Severity and systemic symptoms (nausea) are more consistent with migraine

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Periorbital pain can be caused by sinus disease. However absence of nasal congestion, sinus pressure, purulent nasal discharge, fever, or typical postural worsening argues against sinusitis.
supporting_evidence: Pain localizes around the right eye / periorbital area
opposing_evidence: No nasal symptoms, no fever, no purulent discharge mentioned
Photophobia, visual phenomena and nausea favor migraine

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Intracranial process (mass/space-occupying lesion) or other serious secondary cause
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Progressive headache and difficulty focusing could theoretically reflect a space-occupying lesion. However the short time course (3 days), absence of focal neurological deficits, no morning vomiting, and lack of red flag features make this unlikely in the near term.
supporting_evidence: Worsening headache over several days and cognitive difficulty (difficulty focusing)
opposing_evidence: No focal neurological deficits reported (no weakness, speech issues, vision loss)
No systemic signs (fever), no vomiting, and very acute presentation rather than longer progressive course
Young age and clear migrainous features make primary headache disorder more likely
